content: Triethanolamine (TEA) is a viscous organic compound that functions as both a tertiary amine and a triol, meaning it contains three alcohol groups. It is a strong base and is sometimes referred to as TEOA to differentiate it from triethylamine. While TEA is typically colorless, it may appear yellow due to impurities. Approximately 150,000 metric tons of TEA were produced in 1999. TEA is widely used as an emulsifier and surfactant in both industrial and consumer products. It neutralizes fatty acids, adjusts and buffers pH levels, and helps solubilize oils and other ingredients that are not fully water-soluble. Common applications include liquid laundry detergents, dishwashing liquids, general cleaners, hand cleaners, polishes, metalworking fluids, paints, shaving creams, and printing inks. In cosmetics and medicine, TEA is an active ingredient in certain ear drops, such as those used to treat impacted earwax (e.g., Cerumenex in the United States). It also acts as a pH balancer in a variety of cosmetic products, including cleansing creams, skin lotions, eye gels, moisturizers, shampoos, and shaving foams. TEA-based cleansing milk or cream emulsions are particularly effective at removing makeup. A 1% solution of TEA has a pH of approximately 10, which is significantly higher than the natural pH of human skin (around 5.5–6.0). Regarding safety, TEA has been associated with occasional allergic reactions. A 1996 study reported that TEA can cause contact allergies, while a 2001 study linked TEA in sunscreen to allergic contact dermatitis. A 2007 study found that TEA in ear drops caused contact allergies. A 2008 inhalation study in Wistar rats indicated that TEA has lower systemic toxicity and respiratory tract irritancy compared to diethanolamine (DEA). A 2009 study suggested that patch test reactions to TEA often represent slight irritant responses rather than true allergic reactions, and the risk of skin sensitization to TEA appears to be very low. TEA has also been implicated in tumor development. Studies have shown an increased incidence of liver tumors in female B6C3F1 mice exposed to TEA, though this effect was not observed in male mice or Fischer 344 rats. A 2004 study proposed that TEA may induce liver tumors in mice through a choline-depletion mechanism, likely due to the inhibition of cellular choline uptake. From an environmental perspective, a 2009 study highlighted that TEA exhibits acute, sub-chronic, and chronic toxicity to aquatic species, raising concerns about its ecological impact. In terms of regulation, TEA is listed under Schedule 3, Part B of the Chemical Weapons Convention because it can be used in the synthesis of nitrogen mustards, a class of chemical warfare agents.
